p: Eight years ago, in May of eighteen sixty-seven, Mr John Stuart Mill rose in the House of Commons and moved that, in the Reform Bill then before the House, the word man should be replaced by the word person, so that women householders might vote on the same terms as men. Seventy-three members voted with him. One hundred and ninety-six voted against. The House laughed a good deal during the debate. Two years later Mr Mill published his essay The Subjection of Women, which argues that the legal subordination of one sex to the other is wrong in itself and one of the chief hindrances to human improvement. I have read it twice. I found the first reading irritating and the second persuasive, which is, I suspect, the usual experience of men of my age.

It is worth remembering what that condition was, and in large part still is, in the England of my day. A married woman, under the common law, has no separate legal existence; she and her husband are one person, and that person is the husband. Until the Married Women's Property Act of five years ago, everything she owned, and every penny she earned, belonged to him. She may not easily divorce him. She is excluded from the universities, though a college for women was opened at Hitchin six years ago and has lately removed to Girton, near Cambridge, where its students sit the examinations of the university by private arrangement and may not receive its degrees. She is excluded from the professions; Miss Elizabeth Garrett Anderson qualified as a physician only by discovering a loophole in the rules of the Society of Apothecaries, which then promptly closed it. She may not vote for Parliament or sit in it.

Most of these things have been true of most societies in most ages, and I have described a good many of them in these essays: in Athens, in Rome, under the laws of Hammurabi and of the Church. Yet there were always exceptions and always objectors. Christine de Pizan, a widow of the French court about the year fourteen hundred, wrote The Book of the City of Ladies to answer the slanders of the clerks. Mary Wollstonecraft, in seventeen ninety-two, demanded a Vindication of the Rights of Woman. At Seneca Falls in the state of New York, in eighteen forty-eight, a convention led by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott issued a declaration, modelled upon that of American independence, beginning: we hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men and women are created equal.

The pages from the future tell me how this argument ends, and I shall report it as a historian, though I confess it surprises me by its speed. The first self-governing country in which women will win the right to vote in national elections will be New Zealand, in eighteen ninety-three, after a petition led by a woman named Kate Sheppard, signed by nearly a quarter of the adult women of the colony and pasted together into a roll some two hundred and seventy metres long. South Australia will follow the next year and allow women to sit in its Parliament as well. Finland, then a part of the Russian Empire, will be the first country in Europe, in nineteen hundred and six, and will at once elect women to its assembly.

In England, the campaign will divide. A great body of patient constitutionalists, under Mrs Millicent Fawcett, will petition and lobby for decades. Then, from nineteen hundred and three, Mrs Emmeline Pankhurst and her daughters will found a society whose members the newspapers will call suffragettes, and which will adopt the slogan deeds, not words. They will interrupt meetings, chain themselves to railings, break the windows of the shops of Oxford Street and the government offices of Whitehall, and set fire to empty buildings. Imprisoned, they will refuse food, and the government will feed them by force, through tubes, an operation of great brutality. One of them, Emily Wilding Davison, will run onto the course at the Derby in nineteen thirteen and be struck down by the King's horse, and die of her injuries. Whether their violence helped or hindered the cause is argued by the historians of the future, and I shall not settle it.

What settles it, the Encyclopaedia suggests, is the Great War of nineteen fourteen, of which I shall speak next. When the men went to the trenches, the women went into the munitions factories, onto the trams, into the offices and the fields, and did the work of the nation. In nineteen eighteen, Parliament will give the vote to women over thirty who meet a property qualification, and in nineteen twenty-eight to all women on the same terms as men. The United States will give women the vote in nineteen twenty, France not until nineteen forty-four, and Switzerland, I am amused to read, not in its federal elections until nineteen seventy-one. Some nations of the Arabian peninsula will hold out into the twenty-first century.

The vote was not the end. The women of the future have gone on to demand, and in many countries to win, equal pay, equal access to every profession, and equal treatment in marriage and divorce. They have been prime ministers of Britain, the Encyclopaedia tells me, more than once, and presidents and prime ministers of many other nations. In much of the world the struggle continues. I record all this with the detachment proper to a historian, and add one personal observation. My late wife, who managed my income, my household and my temper for thirty-one years with a skill that no Chancellor of the Exchequer has ever displayed, was not permitted to vote for the members of the Parliament that taxed her. When I put it like that, I find I cannot remember what the argument against it was.
